# Whatever Comes

The coffee is cold now, a thin skin forming on its surface like the Earth's crust millions of years ago. I've been staring at this blank page for twenty minutes, waiting for something to arrive—a thought, a story, a complaint, anything with enough weight to justify sitting here at all. Outside, someone's alarm is going off. A car alarm, relentless and stupid, announcing nothing but its own existence.

I think about whether I should care more about things. Whether the apathy I feel is philosophical resignation or just depression wearing a thinking person's costume. Both, probably. Both at the same time, which is the condition of being alive in 2024 or any year, really. We're always both. We contain multitudes, as someone famous said, and most of them are contradictory and tired.

The coffee skin breaks when I move the cup. That's something. A small change. Entropy is the only honest law.

I'm thinking about my friend Marcus who hasn't texted back in three weeks. Not because anything happened—nothing dramatic. He just got busy with his new job, or his girlfriend, or his own internal weather patterns shifted and suddenly maintaining friendships felt like swimming against a current. I understand this completely. I've done it a thousand times. I'm probably doing it to someone else right now without realizing it. We're all quietly ghosting each other in slow motion, performing presence while absence becomes our actual address.

There's a philosophy to this, I think. Something about how modern life has made us simultaneously more connected and more alone, which is such an obvious observation that I feel stupid writing it, but here it is anyway. The stupid-obvious things deserve repeating because everyone's too cool or too busy to acknowledge them. We're all drowning in group chats and none of us are really talking.

What comes to me, right now, is this: I miss the feeling of being bored in a useful way. Boredom used to be productive. It would drive you to read a book or call someone or go outside. Now boredom is impossible because boredom requires absence of stimulation and absence is not a state we're allowed anymore. There's always something to check, some notification to receive, some person's life to compare against. Boredom has been murdered and replaced with anxiety wearing boredom's clothes.

I wonder what my parents' generation did when they felt like this. Just sat with it, I guess. Looked out a window. Let their minds wander without GPS coordinates. Their emptiness was probably deeper but also less crowded.

The sun is doing that thing where it comes through the window at a perfect angle to make everything look like a photograph of itself. This is the only kind of beauty that feels real to me anymore—accidental, temporary, not performed for an audience. I'm not taking a picture of it. I'm not posting it. I'm just letting it happen and then letting it stop happening, which is what everything does.

I think about all the things I haven't done. Countries I won't visit. Books I won't write. People I won't become. The paths not taken is a cliché because it's true, and we hate true things because they're so common and so useless. Knowing you didn't take the other path doesn't make you feel better about the one you're on.

But here's what I think might matter: there's something almost rebellious about accepting this. About sitting with the not-knowing, the not-having, the not-being. About writing a thousand words that don't go anywhere because sometimes nowhere is exactly where you need to be. The pressure to make everything count, to optimize every moment, to ensure that nothing is wasted—that's the real prison. Freedom might just be the willingness to waste time, to pursue dead ends, to be profoundly mediocre at existing.

The alarm outside finally stopped. The silence after it is louder.

I'm thinking about how strange it is that we're all just here, keeping ourselves alive, feeding our faces and our phones, pretending it means something. And it does and it doesn't. Both. Always both. We're the only animals that need to convince ourselves that existence is meaningful, which suggests it isn't, which is probably fine. Meaning might be a beautiful fiction we invented so we wouldn't panic.

My coffee is completely cold now. The skin is gone. It's just dark liquid in a ceramic cup, which is all it ever was. I could drink it anyway. I probably won't.

What comes to me, at the end of all this non-thought, is gratitude for the simple fact that I got to sit here for a while and waste time productively. That's real. That's something. I got to be bored in a way that mattered because I chose to pay attention to the boredom rather than escape it. I got to be here, with this coffee and this window and this permanent crisis that we call being alive, and I got to complain about it in a way that hurt no one.

The sun is gone from the window now. The day has moved on. It will be night soon and then it will be day again and this will happen until it doesn't. We're all just riding this thing until we're not, and somewhere in between, we try to write something true on a blank page, knowing that truth is the first casualty of clarity.

The alarm will probably go off again tomorrow.

And I'll be here, waiting for something to arrive, even though I'm finally starting to understand that I'm not waiting for anything. I'm already here. I always was.
